title: What If Earth Stopped Spinning? (Second by Second)

segments.text: Right now, you are moving at up to 1,600 km/h. You can't feel it, because everything around you is moving too.
segments.say: Right now, you are moving at up to sixteen hundred kilometres an hour. You can't feel it, because everything around you is moving too.
segments.image: a brightly sunlit planet Earth spinning in space seen from orbit, glowing blue atmosphere, motion streaks of clouds, vivid colours

segments.text: The ground, the air, the oceans. All of it spinning together, once every 24 hours.
segments.say: The ground, the air, the oceans. All of it spinning together, once every twenty-four hours.
segments.image: aerial view of a coastline at golden hour with ocean, clouds and green land, vivid colours

segments.text: So what happens if Earth just stopped? Not slowed down. Stopped. For one second.
segments.image: a giant golden clock frozen in front of planet Earth in space, second hand stopped, cinematic

segments.text: Let's go through it, second by second.
segments.image: a dramatic view of Earth from space at sunrise with a bright sun flare on the horizon

segments.text: At the equator, the ground moves about 465 metres every second. Where Europe and the United States are, it's still over 1,000 km/h.
segments.say: At the equator, the ground moves about four hundred and sixty-five metres every second. Where Europe and the United States are, it's still over a thousand kilometres an hour.
segments.image: a world globe with a glowing golden line along the equator and bright speed arrows pointing east, space background, vivid

segments.text: If the planet stopped in one second, the ground would stop. But you would not. Your body would keep flying east at the same speed.
segments.image: people, cars and trees being flung sideways off a sunny city street by an invisible force, motion blur, dramatic action shot

segments.text: Near the equator, that's a jolt of nearly 50 times the force of gravity. Far worse than any car crash.
segments.say: Near the equator, that's a jolt of nearly fifty times the force of gravity. Far worse than any car crash.
segments.image: a crash test dummy in a car at the moment of impact, glass shattering, dramatic studio lighting

segments.text: Then the air hits. The atmosphere isn't glued to the ground, so it keeps moving too.
segments.image: a gigantic wall of dust and clouds racing across a desert landscape under a bright sky, epic scale

segments.text: That means winds of over 1,000 km/h sweeping around the planet. The strongest gust ever measured was about 408 km/h.
segments.say: That means winds of over a thousand kilometres an hour sweeping around the planet. The strongest gust ever measured was about four hundred and eight kilometres an hour.
segments.image: a violent hurricane hitting a coastal town, palm trees bent flat, sheets of rain, dramatic light

segments.text: Near the equator, the wind would be faster than the speed of sound. Forests, buildings, even loose rock, scoured away.
segments.image: a tropical rainforest being torn apart by a supersonic wind blast, trees ripped from the ground, debris flying, dramatic

segments.text: And the oceans keep moving as well. Walls of water would surge east across the continents, far bigger than any tsunami ever recorded.
segments.image: a colossal turquoise ocean wave crashing over a coastal city skyline in bright daylight, epic disaster movie shot

segments.text: The safest places would be near the North and South Poles, where the ground barely moves at all.
segments.image: a calm bright polar ice landscape with a research station under a clear blue sky, sunlit snow

segments.text: Now imagine Earth didn't start again. The planet still goes around the Sun, but it no longer turns.
segments.image: planet Earth orbiting the Sun seen from deep space, bright sun on the left, dramatic lighting

segments.text: One side faces the Sun, and the Sun creeps across the sky so slowly that one day would last a whole year.
segments.image: a huge sun hanging low and motionless over a desert horizon, long shadows, golden light

segments.text: Six months of daylight. Then six months of night.
segments.image: planet Earth from space split exactly in half, one side in blazing golden sunlight and the other in deep blue night with glowing city lights

segments.text: The day side would bake for months on end. The night side would freeze, colder than Antarctica.
segments.image: split scene: on the left a cracked scorching desert under a blazing sun, on the right a frozen icy landscape under a dark starry sky

segments.text: Without the spin, hurricanes would stop swirling. The weather would become one giant river of air from the hot side to the cold side.
segments.image: satellite view of Earth with long straight streams of clouds flowing from a bright day side to a dark night side, no spiral storms

segments.text: Here's the strangest part. Earth's spin makes it bulge at the middle. It's about 43 km wider at the equator than from pole to pole.
segments.say: Here's the strangest part. Earth's spin makes it bulge at the middle. It's about forty-three kilometres wider at the equator than from pole to pole.
segments.image: planet Earth slightly squashed and bulging at the equator with a glowing ring marking the bulge, space background, scientific illustration style

segments.text: The spin holds the oceans in that bulge. Take the spin away, and over time, the water slides toward the poles.
segments.image: illustration of planet Earth with the oceans flowing away from the equator towards the north and south poles, bright blue water, vivid

segments.text: A giant belt of dry land would rise around the middle of the planet, with a huge ocean at each pole.
segments.image: planet Earth from space with one continuous brown and green continent wrapped around the equator and big blue oceans covering both poles

segments.text: The good news: no. Nothing in the solar system could stop Earth in a second.
segments.image: a peaceful bright view of Earth and the Moon together in space, sunlit, calm

segments.text: But Earth's spin is slowing down, very gently. The Moon's pull on our oceans works like a brake.
segments.image: a full Moon rising over a calm ocean at dusk with a bright tide line on the beach

segments.text: About 1.4 billion years ago, a day on Earth lasted only around 18 hours.
segments.say: About one point four billion years ago, a day on Earth lasted only around eighteen hours.
segments.image: ancient Earth landscape with volcanoes, a rocky shore and a huge bright Moon close in the sky, primordial, vivid colours

segments.text: And the same braking pushes the Moon away from us, about 3.8 cm a year. That's roughly how fast your fingernails grow.
segments.say: And the same braking pushes the Moon away from us, about three point eight centimetres a year. That's roughly how fast your fingernails grow.
segments.image: the Moon slowly drifting away from Earth in space, faint dotted path between them, bright sunlight

segments.text: So Earth will never just stop. It's simply getting a tiny bit lazier every year.
segments.image: a gently spinning planet Earth at sunrise seen from orbit, peaceful, golden light on the atmosphere

segments.text: Which part would scare you most? Tell me in the comments. And subscribe for more things that sound impossible, but are real. Unreal, but true.
segments.image: a person standing on a cliff at sunset looking up at a sky full of stars and a bright planet Earth-like moon, awe, cinematic
